prompt:
Two digital multimeters, Meter X and Meter Y, are tested by measuring the potential difference across a precision reference voltage source whose true output is 5.000 V.
Each meter is used to record five independent readings under identical conditions:
Meter X readings / V: 5.0, 5.0, 5.1, 5.0, 5.0
Meter Y readings / V: 5.142, 5.141, 5.143, 5.142, 5.142
(a) State the instrument resolution of Meter X and Meter Y. [2]
(b) Determine the range of readings for each meter, and state which meter demonstrates higher precision. [2]
(c) Calculate the mean reading for each meter, and determine which meter is more accurate, justifying your conclusion with quantitative calculations. [1]
(d) Explain what modification or adjustment should be applied to Meter Y so that its measurements become both precise and accurate. [1]

parts.description: State resolutions of Meter X and Meter Y
Calculate means and determine which is more accurate
State adjustment to make Meter Y accurate

part_enrichment.guidance: Identify the smallest digit position: one decimal place (0.1 V) vs three decimal places (0.001 V).
Calculate max - min for both meters; compare spread for precision.
Calculate mean for X (5.02 V) and Y (5.142 V); compare difference from true value (5.000 V).
Explain how to subtract the systematic offset (+0.142 V) or recalibrate.

mark_scheme.criterion: Part (a): Resolution of Meter X = 0.1 V (one decimal place).
Part (a): Resolution of Meter Y = 0.001 V / 1 mV (three decimal places).
Part (b): Range for Meter X = 5.1 - 5.0 = 0.1 V; Range for Meter Y = 5.143 - 5.141 = 0.002 V.
Part (b): Meter Y has higher precision because its range / spread (0.002 V) is much smaller than Meter X (0.1 V).
Part (c): Mean of X = 5.02 V (deviation = 0.02 V); Mean of Y = 5.142 V (deviation = 0.142 V). Meter X is more accurate because its mean is closer to the true value of 5.000 V.
Part (d): Recalibrate Meter Y against the standard source or subtract the systematic offset of +0.142 V from all future readings.

hints: In part (a), look at the number of decimal places displayed.
In part (b), compare the ranges: smaller range means higher precision.
In part (c), calculate the difference between each mean and 5.000 V.
In part (d), how do you fix a constant systematic offset?
solution: (a) Meter X resolution = 0.1 V; Meter Y resolution = 0.001 V. (b) Meter X range = 0.1 V; Meter Y range = 0.002 V; Meter Y has higher precision. (c) Mean X = 5.02 V (error 0.02 V); Mean Y = 5.142 V (error 0.142 V); Meter X is more accurate. (d) Recalibrate Meter Y or subtract the +0.142 V systematic offset.
teacher_walkthrough: (a) Meter X displays to 0.1 V, so resolution is 0.1 V. Meter Y displays to 0.001 V, so resolution is 0.001 V.
(b) Spread: Meter X range = 5.1 - 5.0 = 0.1 V. Meter Y range = 5.143 - 5.141 = 0.002 V. Meter Y has a much smaller spread, so it is more precise.
Meter X is more accurate because 5.02 V is closer to 5.000 V than 5.142 V.
(d) Meter Y has a systematic calibration offset of +0.142 V. Recalibrating the meter or subtracting 0.142 V from each reading will make it both precise and accurate.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored comprehensive 6-mark comparative problem analyzing voltmeter data for resolution, precision, and accuracy.
